   84	
   85	### SP2 — The score is normalised against the account, not against absolute numbers
   86	
   87	`utility = goal progress + discounted economic gain + expected profit + information value + schedule fit
   88	− loss risk − fuel and recycler cost − queue and slot opportunity − exposure − broken commitment −
   89	attention cost`, with every term expressed per account-day (a million resources is a different decision
   90	for a three-week account than for a two-year one). This is the shape the plan already commits to.
   91	
   92	### SP3 — Wake at the next material event, never on a fixed period
   93	
   94	**Verified** in three independent projects and it is the single most valuable scheduling idea in the
   95	corpus: compute the next moment at which something could change and sleep until then.
   96	
   97	```
   98	next_wake = min over open work of:
   99	    resource_eta(cheapest ambition)         # missing resources / production per second
  100	    building_finish, research_finish        # the queue countdown
  101	    fleet_arrival, fleet_return             # including an inbound attack's real ETA
  102	    slot_free, storage_threshold, session_window_start
  103	plus a heavy-tailed jitter
  104	```
  105	
  106	PHPOgameBot computes exactly `max(now, resource_eta, build_slot_free, fleet_slot_free, ship_return)`
  107	(**verified**); TBot computes `min(production_time, transport_arrival, returning_expedition) + jitter(SomeSeconds)`
  108	(**verified**); Cruiser pushes an absolute wake at `hostile_arrival − randint(120, 180)` s
  109	(**verified**). The three agree, so this is not taste — it is the mechanism. The jitter must be
  110	heavy-tailed, not uniform: see [H2](#h2-session-shape) and the traps in [H5](#h5-what-makes-a-schedule-look-worse).

  116	(`SessionPlanner::isAwake`). The routine session stays the upper bound, so an event in the dark period

  118	and the `slot_free` (beyond fleet-return) terms remain the deferred refinements, all nameable and

  122	
  123	A planet has one building slot, a player has one research slot and a bounded number of fleet slots.
  124	The corpus's cleanest expression is PHPOgameBot's dependency typing: pending work is grouped by the

 1377	**This is a hard constraint, not a preference.** The host's signal 1 flags an account with **18 or more
 1378	distinct hours-of-day containing a mission departure in a 7-day window**, plus **18+ missions per fleet
 1379	slot per day** and a **50-mission floor**; signal 2 flags an expedition re-dispatched within **10 s** of

 1382	
 1383	```

 1385	every day must contain a dark period of at least 6 consecutive hours
 1386	no reaction is faster than 10 s; no expedition re-dispatch is faster than ~60 s
 1387	```
 1388	
 1389	**Finding.** The general literature agrees with the host's thresholds for the wrong reason and the right
 1390	conclusion: bot detection in MMO traces keys on **periodic peaks** (a WoW bot's keystroke intervals spike
 1391	at exactly 1 s and 5.5 s, its poll timers, while human intervals are Pareto-distributed — **measured**)
 1392	and on inter-action interval *standard deviation* (97% accuracy on one day of data from frequency, mean
 1393	ATI and ATI SD — **measured**). Constant or periodic work, whatever its mean, is the signature.
 1394	
 1395	**As built.** Each account owns one waking window per local day, anchored to a **core wake time drawn
 1396	over 05:30–09:30** so a cohort is early birds and night owls rather than one shift, with a **nine-hour
 1397	core dark period** and up to thirty minutes of drift on either edge. The drift can only *extend* the
 1398	dark period, so the nine-hour core is present every day: eight whole wall-clock hours, which is exactly
 1399	what the host's `COUNT(DISTINCT FLOOR(time_departure % 86400 / 3600))` counts. Sessions are placed only
 1400	inside the window, and a wait that runs into the dark period is spent there rather than shortened.

 1403	seven-day window** against the host's 18, and **14 for the casual persona**; every local day covered by
 1404	a silence longer than six hours; overnight silences of 6–25 hours.
 1405	
 1406	**Accept.** `RoutineCadenceTest` runs the constraint against the module's own clock rather than against
 1407	a live cohort, because the host's signals read *fleet departures* and this is the schedule that produces
 1408	them: it is deterministic, needs no running pilot, and fails the moment the routine can span the hours
 1409	the host flags. Re-run the admin page's three signals against the cohort once fleets exist ([G4](#gap--algorithm-index)),

 1412	### H2 — Session shape
 1413	
 1414	**Shipped 14 September 2026** in `SessionPlanner`, with [H1](#h1-the-active-hours-constraint).
 1415	
 1416	**Gaps:** G10 · **Host:** the schedule (`ai:run-due-work` every minute) and the session runner.
 1417	
 1418	```
 1419	sessions per day:  casual 2–3, active 4–8, one hardcore persona 10–16    (analogue benchmark)
 1420	session length:    heavy-tailed, median 4–8 min, p75 ≈ 15 min,
 1421	                   plus one 45–90 min evening block, never constant      (measured analogue)
 1422	window:            primary 18:00–23:00 local, secondary 12:00–14:00,
 1423	                   sleep 01:00–08:00 local, weekend starts earlier, ends later
 1424	```
 1425	
 1426	**Finding, and the reason the shape matters more than the numbers.** Human inter-event times are
 1427	**heavy-tailed, not Poisson** — email inter-event times follow a power law with exponent ≈ 1
 1428	(**measured**), and web dwell times fit a Weibull with shape `k < 1` on 98.5% of pages, per-category
 1429	median ≈ 0.65–0.80 (**measured**). A uniform or exponential gap distribution is therefore wrong in
 1430	principle: it has bounded support and no long tail. Draw session lengths and inter-action gaps from a
 1431	log-normal or Weibull with `k ≈ 0.7–0.9`, and **derive the next wake from state (S3), not from the last
 1432	wake**.
 1433	
 1434	**As built.** The next wake needs no second mechanism: it is *now + a Weibull wait at shape 0.8*, and a
 1435	session's length is the same draw at the session's own scale. The wait is what the persona's visits per
 1436	day imply (`waking minutes ÷ visits − session minutes`), so the shape is a person's and the rate is the
 1437	persona's. Two rules keep the tail from doing damage: a wait never skips a waking day, and the wait that
 1438	runs into the dark period is **spent** — the account looks in again after waking, on a fresh draw, rather
 1439	than after the overflowed one, which skipped the day it had just woken into.
 1440

 1442	persona, **4.62–6.90** for trader, turtle and miner, **12.05** for the fleeter — inside the benchmark's
 1443	bands above; session length **median 5–8 min, p75 14–19, p90 21–32, longest 40–118 min**.

    /**
     * Whether the account's own clock has come for this item.
     *
     * An accelerated session is claimable the moment its account is awake (that is what shortens the
     * waits), and any item is claimable once its own due time has passed. A session is the exception:
     * the one a session leaves behind is due seconds later, so a worker that is minutes behind finds
     * every session in the cohort overdue, and an overdue session used to be claimable at any hour --
     * which put the whole population online through its own night (AUTH_UPTIME). A session therefore
     * keeps the hour it was scheduled for: only the night session the routine placed in the dark
     * period itself, the reaction wake to an attack landing then, is run at night.
     */
    private function dueForAccount(AiWorkItem $workItem): bool
    {
        if ($workItem->due_at->isFuture()) {
            return $this->acceleratedSession($workItem);
        }

        return $workItem->kind !== AiWorkKind::RunSession || $this->sessionKeepsItsOwnHour($workItem);
    }

    /**
     * A session is the account's own login and happens inside its waking window; the night is spent asleep.
     *
     * A login the worker was late for waits for the next waking day, and so does one that comes due inside the
     * dark period: the routine places every successor inside the window, and both the reaction wake and the
     * material-event wake are deferred when they would land in the night, so no login of the account's own falls
     * there. One that does was moved by something else -- an accelerated backlog, a retry, a maintenance pass --
     * and taking it would put the account online at an hour it sleeps, which is the hour the host's
     * round-the-clock signal counts: an account active in eighteen of the day's hours is not a player (AUTH_UPTIME).
     */
    private function sessionKeepsItsOwnHour(AiWorkItem $workItem): bool
    {
        $profile = $this->workProfile($workItem);

        return $profile === null || app(SessionPlanner::class)->isAwake($profile, now()->toImmutable());
    }
